title: Occasion and date
short: Written on 7 January 1916, when Thomas was training with the Artists Rifles at Hare Hall Camp, Essex; it reworks a prose passage from The Icknield Way (1913).
body: Thomas enlisted in the Artists Rifles in July 1915 and was based at Hare Hall Camp, Gidea Park, near Romford, as a map-reading instructor. The Oxford manuscript of 'Rain' is dated 7 January 1916 and noted as written while travelling home from Hare Hall. The poem returns to a passage in Thomas's travel book The Icknield Way, where the narrator lies awake listening to the 'midnight and solitude of the rain' and hears a ghostly double speak of death; that passage ends with the saying 'Blessed are the dead that the rain rains on'. The opening line, with three 'rain's, sets a heavy incantatory rhythm.

title: this bleak hut
short: An army hut at the training camp: the poem's solitude is that of a soldier in barracks, not of a countryman at home.
body: Soldiers in training in 1915-16 lived in wooden huts in camps like Hare Hall. The word 'bleak' (exposed, cheerless) and the bare list 'and solitude, and me' make the speaker feel stripped to essentials. Readers sometimes assume the poem was written at the front, but Thomas did not go to France until January 1917; the manuscript evidence places it in England. The hut, however, already belongs to the world of war, and the thought of death in the next line is shaped by it.

anchor: Remembering again that I shall die
title: Remembering again that I shall die
short: The rain recalls mortality: the speaker will one day be beyond hearing it, as in the Icknield Way passage.
body: The thought is 'again' because it recurs, and because Thomas had written it before: in The Icknield Way the rain will 'fall darkly upon the grass over the grave when my ears can hear it no more'. In 1916, with the prospect of service abroad, the reflection has a new and literal urgency. The poem's syntax runs on without a break through the next three lines, imitating persistent rain and persistent thought. Thomas was killed at Arras on 9 April 1917.

title: For washing me cleaner than I have been
short: Rain as a baptism or purification; the speaker feels washed cleaner than at any time since birth.
body: The speaker imagines a death in which he could not 'give it thanks / For washing me cleaner than I have been / Since I was born into this solitude'. The rain is a kind of baptism, a purification of the soul as well as the body, with an echo of Psalm 51:7 ('Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow'). But 'born into this solitude' makes isolation the human condition from birth, a recurrent theme in Thomas, who suffered from depression. The Icknield Way passage similarly imagines the rain 'accusing and trying me and passing judgment'.

title: Blessed are the dead that the rain rains upon
short: A folk saying (paired with 'Happy is the bride the sun shines on') shaped like a Beatitude and recalling Revelation 14:13.
body: Thomas had quoted the saying in The Icknield Way (1913) as words he 'used to love, I knew not why'. It belongs to a traditional pairing in which the bride whom the sun shines on and the dead whom the rain falls on are both counted fortunate. Its form echoes the Beatitudes of the Sermon on the Mount ('Blessed are they that mourn', Matthew 5:4) and especially Revelation 14:13, 'Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord . . . that they may rest from their labours'. Rain on a grave was thought a good omen for the soul.

title: here I pray that none whom once I loved
short: The speaker turns from himself to others, praying that no one he loved is lying awake in pain or in sympathy.
body: The colon after l. 7 marks a turn: the speaker's thoughts move to 'none whom once I loved'. 'Once' is chilling, implying that he no longer loves them, which the end of the poem confirms ('no love which this wild rain / Has not dissolved'). The prayer covers the dying, the sleepless and the 'Helpless among the living and the dead', which in early 1916 included the soldiers at the front and those who waited at home.

title: broken reeds
short: Biblical image of frailty ('A bruised reed shall he not break', Isaiah 42:3), here multiplied into myriads: perhaps the dead and broken soldiers.
body: The reed is a biblical emblem of weakness: 'A bruised reed shall he not break' (Isaiah 42:3, quoted of Christ in Matthew 12:20), and Egypt is a 'broken reed' that pierces the hand of whoever leans on it (Isaiah 36:6). Thomas's 'Myriads of broken reeds all still and stiff', with cold water among them, is a desolate natural image that many readers also see as a battlefield of corpses. 'Cold water' contrasts with the cleansing rain earlier. The simile is notoriously hard to construe: it may describe the helpless sympathisers, or the speaker himself ('Like me').

title: Myriads
short: Countless numbers (Greek myrias, ten thousand): the scale of the image suggests mass death.
body: 'Myriad' comes from Greek myrias, 'ten thousand', and in English means an indefinitely great number (OED). In 1916 the word inevitably evoked the vast casualty lists. 'All still and stiff' extends the reeds into an image of rigid bodies, though Thomas never makes the comparison explicit. The heavy stresses and alliteration (still/stiff) slow the line, and the plural noun placed first in the line, before its verbless description, gives it the weight of a casualty statistic rather than an image of nature.

title: no love . . . except the love of death
short: The rain has dissolved every love but one, a love of death; critics differ on whether this is suicidal despair or acceptance.
body: The final sentence admits that all his loves have been 'dissolved' except 'the love of death', a startling statement from a man who had suffered severe depression and once contemplated suicide. The qualification that follows ('If love it be towards what is perfect') turns the feeling into something like a longing for perfection and rest. Some readers find here a death-wish; others see a stoic or quasi-religious acceptance of death as the one thing that 'cannot disappoint'. The Icknield Way passage, where the narrator imagines melting into the rain, supports a reading of surrender rather than despair alone.

anchor: Cannot, the tempest tells me, disappoint
title: what is perfect and / Cannot . . . disappoint
short: Death alone is perfect and cannot disappoint; the storm itself delivers this verdict.
body: The poem ends on 'disappoint', a quiet, almost domestic word for an enormous claim: unlike love and life, death cannot fail to fulfil what it promises. The line break after 'and' leaves the reader hanging before the conclusion, and the parenthetical 'the tempest tells me' gives the rain the voice of an oracle, as the 'ghostly double' does in The Icknield Way. The rain that begins as 'midnight rain' has risen to a 'tempest'. Thomas's preoccupation with death and perfection here can be compared with Keats's 'half in love with easeful Death' (Ode to a Nightingale).

title: Form: blank verse
short: Eighteen lines of blank verse in essentially two long sentences, with the word 'rain' repeated like a refrain.
body: The poem is in unrhymed iambic pentameter, often loosened, with long sentences that run over line endings so that the thought, like the rain, seems unbroken. 'Rain' appears seven times, with 'rains' once more, and 'solitude', 'love' and 'broken reeds' recur, giving an incantatory effect. The last line but one ends on the weak word 'and', an unusual enjambment that enacts suspense. Thomas came to verse late, at Frost's urging, and his blank verse imitates the rhythms of meditative speech rather than formal oratory.
